title: Sentence construction
summary: Build questions, negatives, requests and longer sentences.

lessons.title: Helping verbs
lessons.explain: Helping (auxiliary) verbs work together with a main verb. The main ones are be, do and have. They help to make tenses, questions and negatives. They carry the tense and the subject agreement, so the main verb can stay simple.
structures: Be + verb-ing: She is working.
Do/does/did + base verb: Do you work here?
Have/has/had + past participle: I have finished.
positive: She is studying for an exam.
negative: They have not booked a table.
reallife: At a restaurant: Have you decided what to order?
At work: We are waiting for the manager.

mistakes.wrong: She is work in a bank.
mistakes.right: She works in a bank. / She is working in a bank.
mistakes.why: After is, the verb needs -ing. For a routine, use the present simple without is.
After the helping verb did, the main verb is in the base form.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the helping verb? 'They are playing football.'
exercises.why: Are helps the main verb playing.
Present perfect uses have + past participle.
Does helps with she in a present simple question.

exercises.prompt: He ___ not know the answer. (do / does)

assessment.prompt: Which word is a helping verb in 'I have finished'?
assessment.why: Have helps finished to make the present perfect.

lessons.title: Modal verbs
lessons.explain: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would) add meaning such as ability, permission, possibility, advice or obligation. They are followed by the base verb, never by to or -s.
structures: Subject + modal + base verb: You should rest.
Negative: modal + not: You must not park here.
Question: Modal + subject + base verb?: Can you help me?
negative: You must not use your phone here.
reallife: Giving advice: You should drink more water.
Asking politely: Could you send me the file?

mistakes.why: After a modal, use the base verb with no -s.
Modal verbs are not followed by to.

assessment.prompt: You ___ not smoke in the hospital. (must / are)
assessment.why: Must not shows a strong rule.

lessons.title: Question formation
lessons.explain: To make a question in English we usually change the word order: the helping verb (or be) comes before the subject. In the present simple and past simple we add do, does or did, and the main verb goes back to its base form. For a question about the subject (Who called you?) we do not use do, does or did. The usual order is: question word + helping verb + subject + main verb, as in Where do you live?
structures: Yes/No question: helping verb + subject + main verb: Can you swim?
Wh- question: question word + helping verb + subject + main verb: Where does she work?
Subject question: question word (as the subject) + verb: Who lives here?
negative: Why don't you come with us?
questions: What time does the train leave?
reallife: Asking for directions: Excuse me, where is the bus station? How do I get to the market?
At work: When does the meeting start? Who is joining us?

mistakes.why: Use do, does or did before the subject in present simple and past simple questions.
After does, the main verb stays in the base form.

exercises.why: Question word + does + subject + base verb.

exercises.prompt: What time ___ the shop open? (do / does)
exercises.why: The shop is singular (it), so use does.

exercises.prompt: Which is a question about the subject?
exercises.why: When the question word is the subject, there is no do or did.

assessment.why: After did, use the base form go.

assessment.prompt: How ___ you go to work? (do / does)

assessment.why: Who is the subject, so use wrote without did.

assessment.prompt: What ___ he want for his birthday? (do / does)

assessment.why: With can, put can before the subject and do not add does.

lessons.title: WH questions
lessons.explain: WH questions ask for information. The question words are who, what, where, when, why, which, whose and how. In most tenses the order is: question word + helping verb + subject + main verb.
structures: Wh + do/does/did + subject + base verb?: Where do you live?
Wh + be + subject?: Where is the station?
Who/What as the subject: Who called you? (no do/did)
positive: What time does the film start?
reallife: Meeting someone: Where are you from?
Booking: What time does the train leave?

mistakes.why: A WH question needs a helping verb after the question word.
After did, use the base verb.

exercises.why: We ask about time with when.

exercises.prompt: Which question word asks about a reason?
Choose the correct question about the subject.
exercises.why: When who is the subject, do not use did.

options: What time does the film start?
What time does the film starts?

assessment.prompt: ___ bag is this? It is not mine. (Who / Whose)

options: How do you go to work?
How you do go to work?

assessment.prompt: ___ many people came to the party? (How / What)
Which question asks about a place?

lessons.title: Yes/No questions
lessons.explain: Yes/No questions can be answered with yes or no. To make them, put the helping verb (or be) before the subject. Short answers repeat the helping verb: Yes, I do. No, she isn't.
structures: Do/Does/Did + subject + base verb?: Do you smoke?
Be + subject + ...?: Are you ready?
Modal/Have + subject + ...?: Can you swim? Have you eaten?
reallife: At a shop: Do you have this in a larger size?
At the airport: Is this the right gate?

mistakes.why: In writing and formal speech, use the helping verb before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: Do you like tea? Yes, I like.
mistakes.right: Do you like tea? Yes, I do.
mistakes.why: A short answer repeats the helping verb.

exercises.prompt: Do you speak French? Yes, I ___. (do / am)
Which short answer is correct? 'Is she a teacher?'
exercises.why: The question has is, so the answer has isn't.

assessment.prompt: Did you see the film? No, I ___. (didn't / don't)
assessment.why: The question uses did, so the answer uses didn't.

assessment.prompt: Which short answer is correct? 'Can you swim?'
___ she coming to the party? (Is / Does)

lessons.title: Negative sentences
lessons.explain: To make a negative sentence, add not after the helping verb. In the present simple and past simple, use do not, does not or did not with the base verb. With be, modals and have as helping verbs, put not directly after them. Use only one negative in a sentence.
structures: Present simple: do/does not + base verb: I do not know.
Past simple: did not + base verb: I did not go.
Be/modal/perfect: is not, cannot, have not: She is not here.
positive: I do not like spicy food.
reallife: Refusing politely: I do not want any more, thank you.
Explaining: I did not understand the question.

mistakes.right: I don't know anything. / I know nothing.
mistakes.why: Do not use two negatives in the same clause.
After doesn't, use the base verb.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has a double negative mistake?
options: I don't have nothing to say.
I don't have anything to say.

exercises.prompt: They ___ not at home yesterday. (was / were)

assessment.prompt: We did ___ see the match. (not / no)

assessment.why: Use anybody after a negative verb.

lessons.title: Imperative sentences
lessons.explain: Imperatives give instructions, orders, advice and invitations. Use the base verb with no subject. For a negative imperative, use do not (don't) before the base verb. Add please to be polite, and let's for suggestions.
structures: Positive: base verb: Open the window.
Negative: Don't + base verb: Don't touch that.
Suggestion: Let's + base verb: Let's go.
reallife: Giving directions: Go straight and turn right at the bank.
Instructions at work: Please save the file before you close it.

mistakes.why: An imperative has no subject.
Make a negative imperative with do not or don't.

exercises.why: It gives an order and has no subject.

exercises.prompt: ___ be late for the meeting. (Do not / Not)

assessment.prompt: ___ me your phone number, please. (Give / Giving)

lessons.title: There is / There are
lessons.explain: Use there is and there are to say that something exists or is in a place. Use there is with singular and uncountable nouns. Use there are with plural nouns. Use there was and there were for the past.
structures: There is + singular / uncountable: There is a park. There is some milk.
There are + plural: There are three chairs.
Question: Is there ...? Are there ...?
positive: There is a bank near here.
There are two bedrooms in the flat.
negative: There is not any milk left.
There are not many shops here.
reallife: Describing a room: There is a desk by the window and there are books on it.
Asking: Is there a lift in this building?

mistakes.wrong: There is three books on the table.
mistakes.right: There are three books on the table.
mistakes.why: Books is plural, so use there are.

mistakes.wrong: It has a park near my house.
mistakes.right: There is a park near my house.
mistakes.why: To say something exists, use there is, not it has.

exercises.prompt: There ___ a cat on the sofa. (is / are)
There ___ many people in the park. (is / are)

options: There is some water in the bottle.
There are some water in the bottle.
It has some water in the bottle.
exercises.why: Water is uncountable, so use there is.

options: There are a bus stop here.
There is a bus stop here.
There be a bus stop here.

assessment.prompt: There ___ four seasons in a year. (is / are)
Yesterday there ___ a big storm. (was / were)
assessment.why: A storm is singular and the sentence is past.

lessons.title: Has / Have / Had
lessons.explain: Have is a main verb for possession, experiences and actions (have breakfast). It is also a helping verb for perfect tenses. Use have with I, you, we and they, has with he, she and it, and had for the past. Have as a main verb makes questions and negatives with do.
structures: Possession: I have a car. She has a car. He had a car.
Perfect: I have finished. She has finished. He had finished.
Main verb negative: I do not have time. She does not have time.
negative: I do not have a car.
questions: Did she have a good trip?
reallife: At a pharmacy: I have a sore throat.
Talking about plans: We have a meeting at three.

mistakes.why: Use has with he, she and it.
After do, use the base verb have.

exercises.prompt: We ___ dinner at eight last night. (have)

assessment.why: Had + past participle for an earlier past action.

lessons.title: Do / Does / Did
lessons.explain: Do, does and did are helping verbs for the present and past simple. Use do with I, you, we, they and does with he, she, it. Did is for all subjects in the past. Do can also be a main verb meaning to perform an action (do homework).
structures: Question: Do/Does/Did + subject + base verb?: Does he work?
Negative: do/does/did not + base verb: He did not work.
Main verb: do homework, does the dishes, did exercise.
positive: I do my homework in the evening.
negative: I do not do the cooking.
She did not do her homework.
reallife: Meeting someone: What do you do? I am a nurse.
At home: Did you do the laundry?

mistakes.why: Use does with he, she and it.
After did, use the base verb.

exercises.prompt: In 'She does the shopping', does is a...
exercises.why: Does here means performs, so it is the main verb.

lessons.title: Prepositions
lessons.explain: Prepositions show the relationship between words: place, time and direction. For time, use at (clock times, night), on (days, dates) and in (months, years, parts of the day). For place, use at (a point), on (a surface) and in (inside).
structures: Time: at 5 pm, on Monday, in July.
Place: at the bus stop, on the table, in the box.
Direction: to the market, from home, into the room.
negative: I do not work on Sundays.
questions: What time do you arrive at work?
Where is the key? Is it in the drawer?
reallife: Making plans: Let's meet at the station on Saturday.
Giving directions: The bank is next to the pharmacy.

mistakes.wrong: I will see you in Monday.
mistakes.right: I will see you on Monday.
mistakes.why: Use on with days.
The adjective good takes at.

exercises.prompt: Which preposition is correct? 'The book is ___ the table.'

lessons.title: Conjunctions
lessons.explain: Conjunctions join words, phrases and sentences. Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so) join equal parts. Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when, if, while) join a main clause to a dependent clause that adds information.
structures: and = addition, but = contrast, or = choice, so = result.
because = reason: I stayed in because it rained.
although = contrast: Although it rained, we went out.
positive: She was tired, so she went to bed.
negative: I do not like tea or coffee.
He did not come because he was ill.
questions: Do you want tea or coffee?
reallife: At work: I would call, but I do not have your number.
Making a choice: We can walk, or we can take a bus.

mistakes.wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out.
mistakes.right: Although it was raining, we went out.
mistakes.why: Do not use although and but together.

mistakes.wrong: I stayed at home because of I was tired.
mistakes.right: I stayed at home because I was tired.
mistakes.why: Because is followed by a clause. Because of is followed by a noun.

exercises.prompt: I wanted to go, ___ I was too tired. (but / so)
It was raining, ___ we stayed inside. (so / but)

options: Although he was ill, he went to work.
Although he was ill, but he went to work.
Although he was ill, so he went to work.
Do you want tea or coffee?
I like tea but not coffee.

assessment.prompt: She studied hard, ___ she passed the exam. (so / but)

options: I was late because the bus was slow.
I was late because of the bus was slow.
I was late because the bus slow.

assessment.prompt: I will call you ___ I arrive. (when / but)
We can eat now ___ we can wait. (or / so)

lessons.title: Quantifiers
lessons.explain: Quantifiers tell us how much or how many. Use many and few with countable nouns, much and little with uncountable nouns, and some, any, a lot of and lots of with both. Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions.
structures: Countable: many, a few, few: many books, a few friends.
Uncountable: much, a little, little: much water, a little time.
Both: some, any, a lot of: some tea, any questions, a lot of people.
positive: I have some friends in London.
There is a lot of traffic today.
negative: I do not have any money.
reallife: Shopping: How much is this? Do you have any smaller ones?
Cooking: Add a little salt and a few onions.

mistakes.why: Friends is countable, so use many.

mistakes.right: There is a lot of traffic.
mistakes.why: Traffic is uncountable. Use a lot of or much.

exercises.prompt: How ___ money do you have? (much / many)

exercises.why: Some in a positive sentence; advice is uncountable.

options: I have a lot of time.
exercises.why: Little without a means almost none.

assessment.prompt: I don't have ___ time today. (some / any)

options: She has few friends, so she feels lonely.
She has little friends, so she feels lonely.
She has much friends, so she feels lonely.

assessment.prompt: There is only ___ milk left. (a little / a few)
